messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Error when installing new version of stan
messages.body_plain:
[back on the dev list; Evan, if you're not on the list,
  you should join so you can reply -- this post involves you.]

You should be OK committing it now to the main
branch as long as it doesn't break the way things
currently run.

I'm not sure what you mean by debugging.  I'd like
to sit down and go over what you did for error handling
and matrix operations.

We don't have unit tests for our commands -- they're
a little hard to test that way.  If you created smaller
pieces of code, these should have unit tests.  Daniel or
I can help you with the google test unit-testing framework.

I'm hoping Daniel will be able to add tests of the
full mass matrix version of NUTS to our other model tests.

For turning this into a paper (what you need to do to
get a good job post graduation), what you need to do is
some comparisons with diagonal-adaptation NUTS.
What we're looking for is (a) fast convergence, and (b)
high effective samples per second after convergence.

We can talk more about what specifically to do in the
next meeting.  Evan B. was going to work on some of the
tests for NUTS vs. JAGS.  It's probably best for students
if we produce a series of student-first-authored papers.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: A high dimensional example to compare rotational NUTS with default stan
messages.subject_clean: A high dimensional example to compare rotational NUTS with default stan
messages.body_plain:
We need to understand the full mass matrix adaptation for NUTS
even after we add RM-HMC, because it'll be MUCH faster to run.
We only need to do one estimation and matrix inversion rather than
inverting matrices and calculating third-order derivatives on each
sub-leapfrog step!

Any of the free parameters should be added as command-line options.
For default settings, I think it makes most sense to consider
fully standardized inputs, but we should also talk about this
at the meeting.

- Bob

On 1/2/13 12:08 AM, Yuanjun Gao wrote:
> Dear all,
>
> Happy new year!
>
> I tried to use a correlated multivariate normal distribution to compare the performance of rotational NUTS(both preset the matrix or estimate in the warm-up phase) with default stan. Simulation results shows that default stan does suffer for high correlated parameters while the non-diagonal matrix does provide better results and scales well(even for dimension like 200).
>
> Optimal procedure for estimating a covariance matrix may need more discussion since there are several parameters(like shrinkage parameter and time point for doing the estimation) that are set quite arbitrarily. I am not sure if this is still worth researching since it seems that RMHMC maybe the focus for next semester and hopefully it will tackle those issues.
>
> The report is attached, comments are very welcomed. Thank you very much.
>
>
>
>
>
> Best,
> Yuanjun
>

Using another gcc, RStan could run all example models in Stan.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] large data in R
messages.body_plain:
Looks nice.

The difficulty in applying map-reduce to Stan (what they
call, more descriptive, "divide and recombine"), is
that we don't have any parallelization below the Markov
chain level (unlike the Passage sampler from PRL).
But it would allow us to execute different R functions
on different machines.

It should be really helpful for imputation when you have
many types of missing data and want to impute them
simultaneously.  For instance, you could take all 1000 or 2000
predictors from those big election surveys and impute
the missingness all at once.

It should also be really useful for Andrew's "secret weapon"
(build a bunch of separate models for different groups of
data [and display them together]).

This won't make existing R functions any faster --- you need whole
new conceptions of the algorithms that can be shoehorned
into the map-reduce (what they call, more descriptively,
"divide and recombine").  So you won't just be able to run
lmer for a really large N.  It will make it very easy
to run something like lmer on many small models.  So it'd
be awesome for the "secret weapon" if there were many many
piles of data.

I'm not going to be the first one to say "hree-pay" out loud!

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] large data in R
messages.body_plain:
On 1/5/13 12:58 PM, Michael Betancourt wrote:

> I've always thought that the potential for parallelization is not in HMC itself but in computing the potential and derivatives.  Isn't the passage through the expression graph pretty map-reducable?

That's essentially what Passage does with Gibbs
sampling -- looks at the graphical model and
decomposes it.

And it's what I meant by having to define new
algorithms -- we can't just take Stan as is and
do this.

Forward-mode auto-dif would be much easier.  For
reverse mode, there's a forward expression building
pass then a backward pass. The computation has to
follow the expression graph.  You can't compute
a node on the forward pass until all of its sub-expressions
have been computed.  You can't compute a node on
the reverse pass until all of its super-expressions
have been computed.  There has been a lot of work
in auto-dif on trying to block out bits of the graph
this way in order to reduce the memory entailed by
reverse mode (the idea's to do a bit of forward mode,
then combine into a single reverse mode step).  But
all the algorithms are NP complete and quite hairy.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] model to speed up?
messages.body_plain:
J

Actually, even before the boundary-avoiding priors, you can try running with the variance parameters set to fixed (and reasonable values).  If _that_ is slow, then we have a different sort of computational problem.  If that goes fast, then we can try gradually relaxing the priors until it starts to go wrong.

I disagree with Bob's suggestion that we should be increasing the max number of leapfrog steps.  My intuition is that, if we're taking 1000 steps on this simple hierarchical regression, we need to figure out what's going wrong, rather than trying to solve it using brute force.

A

messages.body_plain:
On Wed, Jan 9, 2013 at 11:44 PM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:

> I disagree with Bob's suggestion that we should be increasing the max number of leapfrog steps.  My intuition is that, if we're taking 1000 steps on this simple hierarchical regression, we need to figure out what's going wrong, rather than trying to solve it using brute force.

Bob's suggestion was for the number of leapfrog steps, not the number of iterations. Perhaps the trajectory isn't getting to the U-turn condition before it maxes out on the number of iterations (given the size of the step). If the model is hitting the boundary here, I think Bob's intuition is right. There may be some other fundamental computational problems with the model, as you point out.

On Jan 9, 2013, at 5:05 PM, Andrew Gelman wrote:

> J
> I'd suggest starting with Bob's suggestions, then another idea is we could throw in boundary-avoiding priors for the sigma parameters, as a computational device to get things moving faster.
> A
>

>> leapfrog steps (2 ^ (depth-1))!  It must be an off-by-one
>> problem on the bound for number of steps in the code.
>> I'll take a look.
>>
>> If you are in fact, hitting the upper limit and getting
>> stuck, you may just be falling back to a random walk
>> and it might help actually increasing the maximum number
>> of leapfrog steps, as counterintuitive as that may sound.

>> It does appear that low variance may be an issue.

>> 95% posterior interval, whereas sigma_gender is

messages.subject: Re: model to speed up?
messages.body_plain:
My NDNUTS(non-diagonal mass NUTS) manages to run 2000 iterations in about 17 minutes. After the warm-up adaptation, the leap-frog per iteration is generally 3,4,5 (I mean, 2^3, 2^4, 2^5).

To better compare the result, I am trying to run the default stan, which only manages to run 300 iterations after 30 minutes. So no doubt my sampler is much faster in this case.

However, in my two runs, one of them is working perfectly with every Rhat smaller than 1.1 while the other does not mixing well(with some Rhat close to 2). Surprisingly, the poor mixing happens to parameters well the correlation is not significant. Like z_state.

I feel that the problem of my sampler is that I am not doing enough shrinkage, so that the limited number of warm-up iterations create some "false" correlation. But I don't have a very good intuition on how much shrinkage I should do and how I should split the warm-up phase. I am afraid that by doing more shrinkage, parameters which do have strong correlation will have a poorer performance.

I was wondering how did you come up with the estimation procedure for diagonal NUTS, especially how did you decide to split the warm-up phase into 10, 20, 40, 80, 160 ,...? Is there some theory or just some empirical result?

Also I am curious about the fact that there can be some parameters with n_eff to be 4000. How can a sampler work so well and how to stan calculate n_eff?

Thank you!

When I was doing the BDA assignments, I will usually drop one of beta's in order to get an identifiable model. For example, I will drop beta_sex for male and only use beta_sex for female. I do know that by doing this I introduce some kind of asymmetry, but at least it runs fast...

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] model to speed up?
messages.body_plain:
Y

e should discuss the nonidentifiabiltiy.  In many cases, nonidentifiability does _not_ slow down the program, all you have to do is monitor convergence on various derived quantities.  See page 465 of my book with Jennifer for some discussion of this point.  But it sounds like you're saying that, in this example, it's actually causing Nuts to take more steps?

In any case, we really don't need to monitor R.hat on the coefficients, only on the derived quantities.

For example, suppose you have a model, y[i] ~ N (mu + tau*alpha[j[i]], sigma), with 3 groups, thus three parameters alpha[j] ~ N(0,1).  In this case, no need to monitor convergence of mu and alpha.  Instead, monitor convergence of mu_adj and alpha_adj, where mu_adj = mu + mean(alpha), and alpha_adj[j] = alpha[j] - mean(alpha) for each j.  To be clear:  mean(alpha) is _not_ the posterior mean. It is the average of the alpha's, that is, (alpha[1]+alpha[2]+alpha[3])/3.

messages.subject: Gaussian processes
messages.body_plain:
I just added a 10-page chapter to the manual on coding
Gaussian processes.  I start with a simple Stan model that
samples from the prior, discuss a Cholesky transform for
efficient multivariate Gaussian generation, extend it to obvious joint model
that can compute the posterior, then to hyperparameter estimation,
then I unfold it with the analytical posterior.  I also do logistic
regression.  So it's quite a few models.  I tested them all
on simulated data.

The examples are in src/models/misc/gaussian-process
and I included R code to generate the data and also run
the examples in Rstan.

It all works surprisingly well, at least up to a few
hundred dimensions.  And it's pretty easy to code in Stan.
(Seeing Yuanjun's code for Andrew's class really helped!)

One issue I was wondering about is how to code the linear
algebra most effectively.  The sources I read (Neal, Rasmussen
and Williams, and MacKay) all do it differently from each other
and from the way I did it.

K: M x N
C: N x N, pos def
y: N x 1
W: M x M

   posterior mean:    K' * inv(C) * y

   posterior covar:    W - K' * inv(C) * K

One approach (what you see from Radford), is to compute

    inv(C) * y = inv(LL') * y

               = L' \ L \ y

I did this the other way around, computing

   K' * inv(C) = K / L / L'

so that I could reuse the computation.

Should I be doing it the other way?  I wouldn't think
it would really matter much because the Cholesky
factorization should dominate on any sizable problem
and the auto-dif on anything smaller.  (These will go
lots faster when I add the partials for matrix division.)

We could add a gaussian_process_sq_exp_log() function
that takes a parameterization of a squared exponential.
Something like this for the prior:

   real gaussian_process_sq_exp_log(vector y, vector x,
                                    real eta_sq, real rho_sq, real sigma_sq);

and this for the posterior:

    real gaussian_process_sq_exp_log(vector y_tilde, vector x_tilde,
                                     vector y, vector x,
                                     real eta_sq, real rho_sq, real sigma_sq);

And we could do the same for the logistic case, though there's
no good analytic optimization for the posterior.  (There are on
the other hand, a whole lot of approximate methods.)

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: Gaussian processes
messages.body_plain:
On Wednesday, January 16, 2013 2:50:55 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> I just added a 10-page chapter to the manual on coding
> Gaussian processes.  I start with a simple Stan model that
> samples from the prior, discuss a Cholesky transform for
> efficient multivariate Gaussian generation, extend it to obvious joint model
> that can compute the posterior, then to hyperparameter estimation,
> then I unfold it with the analytical posterior.  I also do logistic
> regression.  So it's quite a few models.  I tested them all
> on simulated data.

One thing I would add is that in the case where the covariance matrix is fixed, then calculating the Cholesky factorization once and using multi_normal_cholesky(mu, L) only gets you part way to optimum speed because although L is a constant, the inverse of L is calculated repeatedly inside multi_normal_cholesky (except not literally due to the triangular solving). To get optimum speed, you would want to invert L once, transpose that, and do something like this in the model block

lp__ <- lp__ - 0.5 * dot_self(tL_inv * (y - mu));

But when the covariance matrix is a function of unknown hyperparameters, it doesn't make any difference whether you do multi_normal() or multi_normal_cholesky(). Supporting --- or perhaps even providing convenience functions that implement --- various covariance or correlation functions would be nice, although some of them involve special functions that are not implemented in Stan yet and may or may not be in Boost yet.

Ben

spelling this out -- I just didn't know whether to
trust them :-)

I think we should tackle the matrix derivatives first
along the same lines as the products that you (Marcus)
unfolded.

After that, the gain will depend on how much we can
lean on the algebra of the whole problem and save
subcomputations.  I don't think things like vectorization
are going to matter because those matrix ops are a little
more expensive than virtual function calls and a little
pointer chasing.

> factorization once and using multi_normal_cholesky(mu, L) only gets you part way to optimum speed because although L is
> a constant, the inverse of L is calculated repeatedly inside multi_normal_cholesky (except not literally due to the
> triangular solving).

Right.  I'm proud of myself for having figured that
out.  What I meant by the Cholesky transform is that
we generate

   z ~ normal(0,1);  // vectorized

then in the derived quantities block, set the posterior
sample:

    y <- mu + L * z;

where L is just computed once from the fixed covariance
matrix.  At least that's the simple example I used.

 > To get optimum speed, you would want to invert L once, transpose that, and do something like this
> in the model block
>
> |
> lp__ <- lp__ - 0.5 * dot_self(tL_inv * (y - mu));
> |

That makes sense.  I didn't go that far in unfolding
it, but I should mention that.

> But when the covariance matrix is a function of unknown hyperparameters, it doesn't make any difference whether you do
> multi_normal() or multi_normal_cholesky(). Supporting --- or perhaps even providing convenience functions that implement
> --- various covariance or correlation functions would be nice, although some of them involve special functions that are
> not implemented in Stan yet and may or may not be in Boost yet.

Right.  This I also realized, so I wasn't suggesting
it.  The simple example just uses straightup multi_normal,
which I think is easiest to understand.

Michael B's been adding special functions that he needed
for the cumulative distribtuion functions and their
gradients.   There's a lot of opportunity there for
optimization, too, because when we have a truncated

    y ~ Foo(theta) [L,U];

there's often a lot of shared work among the density
Foo, and the two cumulative distribution evals at L and U.
Those optimizations are on the future to-do list.

- Bob

On Jan 17, 2013, at 12:08 PM, Phillip Price wrote:

>
> On Jan 17, 2013, at 8:17 AM, Andrew Gelman wrote:
>
>> . . . remind me to tell you the story of the kosher restaurant.  It's not an amazing story but it has a small twist with statistical content!
>
> Good. Let's speak soon.
>
> I'm using Stan! Perhaps this means I should have been using BUGS all along, but the last time I tried to use it for one of my current problems, a few years ago, it was just so slow that I gave up. The problem isn't how long it takes to run once I have a model --- if I had a good model I could tolerate taking four or five days for it to run--- it's that the development cycle was so long. I would work with a much smaller dataset than I really wanted to use, to try to speed things up, and then I would add something to the model and test it, and it would be slow even on the small dataset... I couldn't test more than one change per two days or something. Eventually I concluded that the vastly more complicated models that I really wanted to fit were simply untenable.
>
> But with Stan it's going great, to the point that I keep wondering if I'm somehow missing something and the results aren't as good as I think they are.  Basically I am trying to fit a model that captures most of what I know about my problem. This results in a model with considerably more parameters than data points (of the order of 7000 of each), but with pretty tight constraints on the parameters or on combinations of them, through a moderately complicated model structure. I knew it would be possible in principle to fit this but I thought that in practice it might require a too delicate balance of  distributional assumptions and prior estimates: I thought I'd end up overfitting, or underfitting, or something. But no, so far so good. It is such a big change in the models I am trying to fit that it seems qualitative rather than just quantitative, the way going from Conestoga wagons to jet airplanes isn't just a quantitatively faster way to cross the country.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Re: Gaussian processes
messages.body_plain:
On Thursday, January 17, 2013 6:39:31 PM UTC, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> On 1/16/13 5:57 PM, Ben Goodrich wrote:
>
> > On Wednesday, January 16, 2013 2:50:55 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>
> >
>
> >     I just added a 10-page chapter to the manual on coding
>
> >     Gaussian processes.  I start with a simple Stan model that
>
> >     samples from the prior, discuss a Cholesky transform for
>
> >     efficient multivariate Gaussian generation, extend it to obvious joint model
>
> >     that can compute the posterior, then to hyperparameter estimation,
>
> >     then I unfold it with the analytical posterior.  I also do logistic
>
> >     regression.  So it's quite a few models.  I tested them all
>
> >     on simulated data.
>
> >
>
> >
>
> > One thing I would add is that in the case where the covariance matrix is fixed, then calculating the Cholesky
>
> > factorization once and using multi_normal_cholesky(mu, L) only gets you part way to optimum speed because although L is
>
> > a constant, the inverse of L is calculated repeatedly inside multi_normal_cholesky (except not literally due to the
>
> > triangular solving).
>
>
>
> Right.  I'm proud of myself for having figured that
>
> out.  What I meant by the Cholesky transform is that
>
> we generate
>
>
>
>    z ~ normal(0,1);  // vectorized
>
>
>
> then in the derived quantities block, set the posterior
>
> sample:
>
>
>
>     y <- mu + L * z;
>
>
>
> where L is just computed once from the fixed covariance
>
> matrix.  At least that's the simple example I used.
>
>
>
>  > To get optimum speed, you would want to invert L once, transpose that, and do something like this
>
> > in the model block
>
> >
>
> > |
>
> > lp__ <- lp__ - 0.5 * dot_self(tL_inv * (y - mu));
>
> > |
>
>
>
> That makes sense.  I didn't go that far in unfolding
>
> it, but I should mention that.
>
>
>
> > But when the covariance matrix is a function of unknown hyperparameters, it doesn't make any difference whether you do
>
> > multi_normal() or multi_normal_cholesky(). Supporting --- or perhaps even providing convenience functions that implement
>
> > --- various covariance or correlation functions would be nice, although some of them involve special functions that are
>
> > not implemented in Stan yet and may or may not be in Boost yet.
>
>
>
> Right.  This I also realized, so I wasn't suggesting
>
> it.  The simple example just uses straightup multi_normal,
>
> which I think is easiest to understand.
>
>
>
> Michael B's been adding special functions that he needed
>
> for the cumulative distribtuion functions and their
>
> gradients.   There's a lot of opportunity there for
>
> optimization, too, because when we have a truncated
>
>
>
>     y ~ Foo(theta) [L,U];
>
>
>
> there's often a lot of shared work among the density
>
> Foo, and the two cumulative distribution evals at L and U.
>
> Those optimizations are on the future to-do list.
>
>
>
> - Bob

I spend all my time using gaussian processes with MCMC.

It is quite surprising where the time is spent. Constructing K and C can be a bottleneck in some cases.

Realising what is dependent and independent on x (the current position) is vital, and storing intermediate vectors of things which are independent of x.

I don;t have time to understand Bob's notation, but my guess is that K is dependent on x and inv(C) * y  is independent. So most of the work will be spent in repeatedly contsructing K, little work is done in cholesky factorisation or back substitution, at least for the mean. The variance does need repeated back substitutions.

Of course, to calculate

K' * inv(C) * K

one should calculate

P = L \ K

and then construct

P' * P

There are as many varieties of gaussian processes as there are names. Surrogate, proxy, linear bayes, estimator, radial basis function, etc etc.

There are many flavours of the algorithms. I come more from a linear bayes perspective. I also pay significant attention to a linear regreassion model as a starting point, with second order terms. I use sophisticated techniques to determine the efficient terms in the polynomial.

There are issues such as whether one should include the variance of the regression beta coefficients on the variance.

I actually use Matern correlation functions rather than gaussian. They are more flexible but more time consuming, unless (as i do) you use approximate methods. Taking the derivatives of matern adds extra complexity...

There is another range of choices in the hyperparameters, you can go from one global correlation length to adapting every term in the correlation matrix - but rasmussen discusses these alternatives quite well.

As a point of note, I caculate all the derivatives and use NUTS very successfully.

A lot (all?) of the computation can be easily vectorised. This is where R is excellent, at things like matrix * matrix calculations. I don;t know exactly what underlying libraries they use, but some version of BLAS must be there. A C implementation should use similar libraries.

We don't pay anything for vectorized vs. unvectorized
loops because Stan loops are compiled to C++ loops.

Having said that, we're using the Eigen C++ lib, which
indeed does efficient matrix ops and linear algebra.

The big deal for us is vectorizing things that involve
the gradient (that is, involve estimated parameters),
because they can dramatically cut down on virtual function
calls, memory fiddling (we manage our own in an arena-based
arrangement), and the size of the expression graph.

- Bob

Maybe we are talking with different ssumptions, but....

I am talking about sampling a single Gaussian process using MCMC.

So if we have nS samples, for the mean we do cholesky factorisation 1 time, we construct the k matrix nS times, and we multiply the K matrix by the stored constant vector nS times.

The K matrix takes nData x dimension operations.

So in total the K matrix contruction dominates, it take O(S x dimension x data points) operations.

That is for the mean. The variance is different, of course, you have to do a lot of back substitutions, but again factorisation is only done once for all samples.

Maybe you are talking about optimising the hyper parameters, where of course you have to factorise each time they change.

It is late and i am tired so I may be wrong, I have not checked against my code, but more likely we are talking about different things. If in doubt I can send some profiling results.

messages.subject: no-U-turn condition on diagonal mass matrix?
messages.subject_clean: no-U-turn condition on diagonal mass matrix?
messages.body_plain:
If I understand Michael B correctly, there's currently
a (serious?) issue in the way the no-U-turn condition
is defined for our default mode of operation (diagonally
adapted NUTS).

Quick question:  does this destroy detailed balance or just
negatively impact efficiency?

I don't have an opinion on how this one gets resolved,
but I was hoping that Michael and Matt could put their
heads together and come to some kind of agreement on what
fix is needed.  I'm happy to pitch in on the coding and
testing side.

Given this and the fact that smoothing hasn't been
finalized (or has it?) for the full mass matrix adaptation,
I haven't tried to merge Yuanjun's branch into the trunk.
But I'd really really like to get it in sooner rather than
later because of how well it seemed to work for Jiqiang's
multilevel GLM.

Given that we're working on more mass-matrix related approaches,
all else being equal it's simpler conceptually (both for me to
understand and for the doc) if we could use the mass matrix
approach everywhere.

- Bob

messages.subject_clean: [stan-dev] no-U-turn condition on diagonal mass matrix?
messages.body_plain:
Detailed balance is not destroyed. NUTS's detailed balance relies on
only two aspects of the leapfrog integrator:
1. reversibility
2. volume-preservation
both of which are preserved by nuts_diag (once it stops adapting, of course).

The criterion for nuts_diag is the classic U-turn criterion, which is
probably suboptimal—it should probably do the transformation implied
by using different step sizes when computing its dot products.

Matt

I suspect that for nuts_diag (and nuts_nondiag) the correct U-turn criteria is to check the dot product between the gradient and the velocity vector (i.e., inverse mass matrix times momentum) which I think is what Matt is proposing.

For the identity mass matrix case, these two dot products would have the same sign (if not the same magnitude) so it didn't matter then. It should be a relatively easy fix.

On Jan 18, 2013, at 4:44 PM, Matt Hoffman wrote:

> The criterion for nuts_diag is the classic U-turn criterion, which is
> probably suboptimal—it should probably do the transformation implied
> by using different step sizes when computing its dot products.

Correct, this is about what Yuanjun was concerned.  Should be a simply fix for the current code (add the current step-size vector as a parameter to the criterion function and do an entry wise product before projecting onto p).

For dense mass matrix computations the multiple step-size trick is no longer valid and we'll have to appeal to the full P = (L^{T})^{-1} p, Q = L^{T} q transform.

That took longer to e-mail about than to code
and test :-)

Here's what I did.  I haven't committed yet:

       inline static bool compute_criterion(std::vector<double>& xplus,
                                            std::vector<double>& xminus,
                                            std::vector<double>& mplus,
                                            std::vector<double>& mminus,
                                            std::vector<double>& step_sizes) {
         std::vector<double> total_direction;
         stan::math::sub(xplus, xminus, total_direction);
         for (size_t i = 0; i < total_direction.size(); ++i)
           total_direction[i] /= step_sizes[i];
         return stan::math::dot(total_direction, mminus) > 0
             && stan::math::dot(total_direction, mplus) > 0;

           criterion = compute_criterion(xplus, xminus, mplus, mminus,_step_sizes);

using step_sizes_[i] in the definition.  Any reason to prefer one approach
the other?  I know I should favor local variables, but this involves
sending in a reference, whereas the member variable is just a plain
old std::vector<double>.

Dear Bob,

I think the new code is the right one.

I am not quite familiar with the static member function. I am just a little worried because for nondiag_nuts and maybe Geonuts, we will need to use another version of stopping criterion, which uses a mass matrix rather than a step-size vector(although I didn't fully understand what kind of stopping criterion is Geonuts using...). Will these functions conflict with each other when both are claimed to be static and are using the same name? I am worried because when I try to use the new stopping criterion function which is claimed to be static, the compiler complains.

I do think that the Neal's trick can be generalized to densed mass matrix(the detail of which is attached). We just need substitute the step-sizes to the Cholesky decomposition(and sometimes the transposition of the decomposition) of the mass matrix. Originally I find this trick quite useful because  this trick doesn't require any matrix inversion at all, but now it turns out that in order to compute the stopping criterion, a matrix inversion is inevitable, so maybe that trick won't bring efficiency to the algorithm.

Right now I changed my criterion in nondiag_nuts to be

      inline bool compute_criterion(std::vector<double>& xplus,

                                           std::vector<double>& xminus,
                                           std::vector<double>& mplus,

                                           std::vector<double>& mminus) {

        std::vector<double> total_direction;
        stan::math::sub(xplus, xminus, total_direction);

        Eigen::Map<Eigen::VectorXd> total_direction_mat(&total_direction[0],total_direction.size());
        Eigen::Map<Eigen::VectorXd> mplus_mat(&mplus[0],mplus.size());
        Eigen::Map<Eigen::VectorXd> mminus_mat(&mminus[0],mminus.size());
        _cov_L.triangularView<Eigen::Lower>().solveInPlace(total_direction_mat);
        return total_direction_mat.dot(mplus_mat) > 0
          && total_direction_mat.dot(mminus_mat) > 0;
      }

which I am quite sure is the right thing.

You can't have two functions with the same fully
qualified name.   The fully qualified name includes
the namespace, and if it's a member function (non-static
function defined within a class or struct), the name
of the class, plus the function name + the argument
type sequence.  The return type doesn't matter.

So you just need to name your function something else.
Or make it a non-static member function.

You could probably make this a bit more efficient by
passing in a reference to an Eigen::VectorXd to
a slightly differently defined stan::math::sub() that populates
it directly.

void stan::math::sub(..., Eigen::VectorXd& total_direction) {
    ... write into total_direction ...

Then you can call it presized (which you should also do with total_direction
std::vecotr if you leave it the way you have it):

   Eigen::VectorXd total_direction(xplus.size());

   stan::math::sub(xplus, xminus, total_direction);

I'd also suggest renaming variables that you call _mat
to _vec, because although it's technically correct that
everything's a matrix in Eigen, I found it confusing reading
the code.

In fact, compute_criterion could itself be changed to
use Eigen vectors rather than std::vector.  It would make
much of the new code cleaner (wouldn't require the
map wrappers and all that reference to first array business,
which is the only way to do things now).

We could actually rewrite everything to use Eigen vectors,
which would probably be more efficient.  I wrote it the way
it is now thinking we could write almost everything without
a dependency on Eigen (for instance, if you look at the model
specifications, they only depend on std::vector, not on anything
in Eigen).  But since then, for both efficiency
and for expressiveness, we've used more and more of Eigen
throughout the mcmc package.  So I don't think it's worth
worrying about keeping all these things separate.  The same
thing happened to intertwine the probability classes and
the auto-dif classes.

- Bob

messages.subject: programming languages
messages.body_plain:
To lay some ugly rumors to rest,

* functional languages are not slow compared to
   object-oriented languages,

* each language has its strengths and weaknesses ranging from
   speed to library availability to portability to
   size of developer community to steepness of learning curve,

* as of the later 1.6 JVMs, Java is pretty close to C++
   in basic arithmetic, array operations, function dispatching,
   etc.,

* Fortran and some functional languages (like ML) and some styles
   of C++ programming with templates can be very fast because
   the compiler can do so much static resolution,

* folded code can be surprisingly fast in Java due to the
   just-in-time compiler's ability to dynamically unfold loops
   based on run-time analysis, and

* interpreted languages (Python, R, MATLAB) are very slow to loop
   and make function calls, but if one function call does a lot
   of work (typically calling vectorized operations in Fortran or C(++)),
   then the added efficiency of a compiled language may not even
   be noticeable.

What is slow is

* unpredictable branch points,

* including virtual function calls (including most Java non-static
   method calls, C++ virtual function calls, C function
   pointer calls), and

* accessing memory out of order.

- Bob

P.S.  I can almost always be baited into a programming language
       discussion.  So please, help me stop.

> trying to minimize it. The only thing I would add is that I think an Eigen::Matrix<> or Eigen::Vector<> should be used
> instead of std::vector<> iff linear algebra is involved.

There's always been a dot product involved.  It'll let us
remove some functions if we use Eigen.  And the Eigen ones
may be a bit more efficient because they're pretty careful
on the implementation details.

 > If it is just holding values or being utilized elementwise,
> then an Eigen::Array<> should be used.

What's the advantage of Array?  I thought Array and
Matrix were lightweight wrapper classes holding a pointer
to the data and dimensions.  I know that Array supports
more elementwise ops and fewer matrix ops, but I'd think
they'd be of the same efficiency.

I really like how Eigen lets you map its data, so it's
pretty cheap to convert back and forth (just a constructor
call).

- Bob

messages.subject: added HMMs, measurement error, meta-analysis
messages.body_plain:
I added models and a chapter to the manual on
measurement error and meta-analysis.  I followed
the definitions in BDA pretty closely.

I also added HMMs, including a model for simple
supervised parameter estimation and a model for
full Bayesian prediction (aka semi-supervised
training or even unsupervised training).  It only
needs the forward part of forward-backward,
unlike EM which needs full forward-backward to compute
summary statistics in the E step.  I even coded up
a first-best Viterbi decoder in a generated quantities
block.  Now I need to find some examples for testing
and write the manual chapter :-)

- Bob

messages.subject: bug in comparison operator code generation
messages.subject_clean: bug in comparison operator code generation
messages.body_plain:
In release 1.1.0, the comparison operators are compiled
to the wrong targets.  Specifically, > is compiled to >=
and vice-versa and < to <= and vice-versa.

I just pushed a patch to the trunk on git.

This motivate us to get the next version out ASAP.

Until then, there's not really a good workaround.

(This one's all my fault -- I had to rearrange the
order to deal with Boost Spirit's greedy parsing
strategy, but I forgot to take the semantic actions
along with the operator literals.)

- Bob

the current unadjusted U-turn condition and the
one adjusted for step sizes.

The frightening part of the results is that just
measuring the parameters with the minimum n_eff,
you see variation of a factor of 10 from run to
run of the same sampler.  You also see variations
like that between the samplers.

The mean and median n_eff are more stable.

This has serious implications for how we're going to
measure and report timings.  I'm not sure what it
means for measuring convergence.  Sometimes the param
with the min n_eff has an n_eff of 2 or 5 when the
max has an n_eff of 2000.  Clearly the params aren't
mixing equally well.

I'll need to run more tests to get a sense of
the trends and variations.

I've attached three runs of the output in .csv format.
The new is the adjusted one, and I ran once in clang++
and once in g++.

- Bob

messages.subject: need 3rd party sources for Wikipedia
messages.body_plain:
I created the Wikipedia article for Stan, but
we don't have any of what Wikipedia calls "reliable
3rd party sources" for the information.

We need the NUTS paper to be published.  Matt -- is
there anything the rest of us can do to help
get it out?

It would also help if we had something published
on Stan per se.  It would create "legitimacy"
for people who only believe something if it's
peer reviewed.

The only citation for JAGS is a workshop paper,
and the citations for WinBUGS and OpenBUGS are
similarly minimal:

   http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Just_another_Gibbs_sampler

   http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WinBUGS

   http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/OpenBUGS

So we might have been OK if the text for the
workshop paper on prob computing at NIPS were
available publicly.  I couldn't find it, though.

- Bob

>
> I believe that one of the size tests is failing
> (mu must be same size as y, and the rows and columns
> of Omega must be the same).
>
> This is puzzling given your model, the declarations
> for which are
>
> >      matrix[nData, nVars] y;
> >      matrix[nData, nVars] mu;
> >      cov_matrix[nVars] Omega;
>
> seem to me to be compatible with the usage:
>
>
> >        col(y, i) ~ multi_normal(col(mu,i), Omega);
>

I believe this should be:

row(y, i) ~ multi_normal(row(mu,i), Omega);

In the above, col(y,i) and col(mu,i) are vector[nData] but Omega is cov_matrix[nVars].

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.body_plain:
Peter,

Write the binomial coefficient as a product of logs (or a sum of log gammas) and then use the digamma function (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polygamma_function).  Same for lngamma.  Boost provides a convenient implementation (http://www.boost.org/doc/libs/1_52_0/libs/math/doc/sf_and_dist/html/math_toolkit/special/sf_gamma/digamma.html).

-Mike

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Forward-Mode Auto Diff Problems
messages.body_plain:
On 1/31/13 8:28 AM, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> Peter,
>
> Write the binomial coefficient as a product of logs (or a sum of log gammas) and then use the digamma function (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polygamma_function).  Same for lngamma.  Boost provides a convenient implementation (http://www.boost.org/doc/libs/1_52_0/libs/math/doc/sf_and_dist/html/math_toolkit/special/sf_gamma/digamma.html).

In general, you can crib off what we did for agrad/agrad.hpp
and agrad/special_functions.hpp.

Some more below.

> On Jan 30, 2013, at 11:53 PM, Peter Li wrote:
>
>> Hi,
>>
>> I'm currently working on the forward-mode auto diff and I have 3 questions/problems:
>>
>> 1) I'm not sure how to approach binary_log_loss, binom_coeff_log, and lmgamma.

Just look at the definition of the functions (which you'll
find, if nowhere else, in the agrad/agrad.hpp and agrad/special_functions.hpp
doc for the functions) and then calculate the partials with respect to
the arguments.

I've been trying to add more mathematical definitions to the doc.
I just added log loss, because that's the least standard of the
above.  I'd like to also add all their partials with respect to
their arguments to the doc.

The Wikipedia page on gamma gives you the derivative of
the gamma function in terms of the digamma function (also
available in Boost and used in stan/agrad/special_functions.hpp),
so you just use the chain rule to figure out the derivative
of log gamma.

You'll also find the definition of binary_log_loss in the
doc in the agrad files.

>> 2) For fmin/fmax, I am getting an error that "fmax" is ambiguous when I have something like fmax(x1.val_, x2.val_). I think this is because there is no fmax method for double, double. I tried to add one to stan/agrad/special_functions, but I keep getting an error.

Can you dump out more of the error message you're getting
for fmax().  The rule is that the arguments have to uniquely
specify a function implementation and there's a long chain
of rules to figure out which of those functions it is.  If
the compiler's telling you it's ambiguous, then there are
two equally acceptable definitions.

You can use explicit naming to disambiguate, for instance
explicitly using the double-based implementation of fmax
boost::math::fmax(x1.val_,x2.val_).

>> 3) I've also run into a problem with Phi (described below).

This is the key error message:

 >> lib/boost_1.52.0/boost/math/special_functions/erf.hpp:123:9: error: invalid
 >>       operands to binary expression ('stan::agrad::fvar<double>' and 'int')
 >>    if(z < 0)

You need to define the comparison operators for fvar
and templated alternative types.

- Bob

messages.subject: atan2 autodiff issue: fixed
messages.body_plain:
Michael hunted it down.

The autodiff was not implemented properly for reverse mode. It needed to include the current adjoint in the derivative.

Our guess is that fmod will have the same problem.

We added a test to the agrad tests for atan2 (var, var) that inserts the node into another expression. We did it by multiplying by a double and making sure the derivatives propagated the constant term through. We should do this for all special functions to catch these sorts of issues.

Daniel
